scenarios.label: Lower
scenarios.name: lower scenario
scenarios.title: Sluggish adoption
scenarios.text: Wisconsin performs like the slowest statewide reforms so far, Rhode Island and Oregon (average about 0.77 permits per 1,000 single-family homes per year once the law is fully in force).
scenarios.info: The average of the two slowest statewide-law states, Rhode Island (0.84) and Oregon (0.71): about 0.77 permits per 1,000 single-family homes per year at a typical place once the law is fully in force (4 years or more), 0.6486 of the central level. Every Wisconsin place's central level is multiplied by that factor, so the differences between places stay the same. Rhode Island has only one year of data after its law (2025), so its level rests on one year. At Gate 3 the lower was the 10th percentile of the states' spread (central ÷ 1.80); that is now a sensitivity case. In 2027–2029 the addition reaches 0.62, 0.83, 0.85 of its full size; full from 2030. No Wisconsin place goes below a minimum rate set from Madison's own permits (0.2345 per 1,000 single-family homes per year: Madison's 2022–2025 rate of 0.1876 divided by 0.8). Madison itself follows the path of similar cities in Washington and Oregon in every scenario.
scenarios.basis: Like the slowest statewide-law states (owner decision 2026-10-26, AQ-043): the mean of Rhode Island's (0.8484) and Oregon's (0.6997) stage-2 levels, 0.7741 permits per 1,000 single-family homes per year at a typical place with the law in force 4+ years, = 0.6361 of the common level 1.2169 (AQ-061 refit; was 0.6497 of 1.0035). Every area's central level is multiplied by 0.6361 (same within-state differences). Ramp: the pooled ramp recomputed for this level the way the central and upper ramps were (homes-weighted, on the adopted current-law rates since AQ-061), not Oregon's observed ramp. Replaces the 10th percentile of the between-state spread (factor 1/1.885), now a sensitivity case.

scenarios.label: Central
scenarios.name: central scenario
scenarios.title: Typical adoption after a statewide ADU law
scenarios.description: Typical adoption after a statewide ADU law
scenarios.text: Wisconsin performs like most of the eight states with a statewide ADU law: about 1.19 permits per 1,000 single-family homes per year once the law has been in force 4 years (Maine 1.36, Utah 1.26, Massachusetts 1.17). California is one of the eight and counts toward this typical level, yet the level sits far below California's own 2.41.
scenarios.info: The common level of the eight statewide-law states (California included), about 1.19 permits per 1,000 single-family homes per year at a typical place once the law has been in force 4 years. Wisconsin's statewide rate comes from that level and Wisconsin's mix of home values, incomes and sizes; it is then spread across places by home value alone, as places differ within the eight states. In 2027–2029 the addition reaches 0.63, 0.83, 0.86 of its full size; full from 2030. No Wisconsin place goes below a minimum rate set from Madison's own permits (0.2345 per 1,000 single-family homes per year: Madison's 2022–2025 rate of 0.1876 divided by 0.8). Madison itself follows the path of similar cities in Washington and Oregon in every scenario.
scenarios.basis: Like a typical statewide-law state: pooled revision (ii) configuration A central; ramp from the pooled year terms

scenarios.text: Wisconsin does better than every statewide-law state except California: about 2.15 permits per 1,000 single-family homes per year once the law has been in force 4 years. Only California has gone higher (2.41), and its laws go beyond the benchmark in several ways (ADUs on apartment properties, more than one ADU per lot), so this is the high end of the expected range.

In 2027–2029 the addition reaches 0.63, 0.83, 0.86 of its full size; full from 2030. No Wisconsin place goes below a minimum rate set from Madison's own permits (0.2345 per 1,000 single-family homes per year: Madison's 2022–2025 rate of 0.1876 divided by 0.8). Madison itself follows the path of similar cities in Washington and Oregon in every scenario.
scenarios.basis: Strong adoption: pooled revision (ii) configuration A, 90th percentile of the between-state spread (factor 1.83 after the AQ-061 refit). The high end of what statewide-law states have reached; only California has gone higher.

reference_line.label: Median performance in 8 examples of statewide ADU reform
reference_line.info: The middle (median) of what the 8 states with a statewide ADU law, California included, actually permitted in each year after their law, applied to Wisconsin's single-family homes. It is a check on the scenarios, not a scenario.
reference_line.detail: States with data in each year after the law: year 1 (2027): 7, VT 0.6435, WA 0.7696, OR 0.7778, MA 1.0073, RI 1.1261, ME 1.2444, CA 1.5165; year 2 (2028): 4, VT 0.7873, OR 0.9511, UT 1.2998, CA 2.3876; year 3 (2029): 4, VT 0.7583, OR 0.8777, UT 1.1684, CA 2.9682; year 4 (2030): 4, OR 0.8740, UT 1.3857, VT 1.3862, CA 3.2528; year 5 (2031): 1, CA 3.4246. Drawn through 2030; 2031 carries 2030 forward (dashed), because only one state has that many years of data. Non-California series leave out ADUs built with a new house on an empty lot (× 0.951); California's counts use the cap of 2 ADUs per parcel and the multifamily-lot rule. Median rates: 1.01, 1.13, 1.02, 1.39, 1.39 permits per 1,000 single-family homes per year in 2027–2031. Added permits over the observed years only (2027-2030): 7,931. Series: reference/adu_model_reference_line_by_year.csv (8_state_median).
reference_line.why_central_differs: The central scenario (10,679 added permits) and this line (10,374) are built differently. The line applies one median state rate to every Wisconsin home. The central scenario gives each place the level that similar places reached in the eight states (by home values, incomes and size), with a ramp-up in the first three years, and no place below a minimum rate set from Madison's permits.

page_intro.compare: This page shows how many permits for second homes on single-family lots (accessory dwelling units, or ADUs, and conversions of a house into a duplex) Wisconsin can expect if the statewide benchmark ADU law takes effect on 1 January 2027. It shows a baseline of how many would be permitted without the law, and then three scenarios for the bottom, middle and top of what we expect, based on how statewide reform has rolled out in other states. They are scenarios, not confidence intervals: each one describes a way Wisconsin could respond, not a statistical probability.
